canonFrame.defaultEra: 576 CY, the classic and 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide baseline
canonFrame.editionAssumptions: Use the Greyhawk chapter of the 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide as the current accessible baseline. It deliberately returns to a 576 CY framework inspired largely by the original World of Greyhawk presentation and treats the setting as a foundation the Game Master can customize. Use original first-edition gazetteer material as deep support. Treat later Greyhawk Wars, From the Ashes, Living Greyhawk, and other advancing timelines as optional overlays rather than automatic history.
canonFrame.timelineNotes: Greyhawk has several heavily developed publication eras. The 576 CY baseline presents the Flanaess before the major continent-wide changes of the Greyhawk Wars. Later sources advance rulers, borders, destroyed states, and faction power. Do not blend 576 CY with 585 CY, 591 CY, Living Greyhawk outcomes, or organized-play developments without an explicit campaign choice.

campaignFoundations: Greyhawk centers on the Flanaess, the eastern portion of the continent of Oerik on the world Oerth.
The setting favors political volatility, dangerous wilderness, ancient ruins, morally mixed states, and ambitious individuals.
The Free City of Greyhawk is an important adventuring and commercial center but does not rule the Flanaess.
No single empire controls the region; kingdoms, city-states, theocracies, nomads, humanoid realms, and declining empires compete.
Iuz, the Great Kingdom, the Scarlet Brotherhood, the Horned Society, and other threats have distinct methods and territories.
Ancient Suel, Baklunish, Flan, and Oeridian histories continue to shape language, culture, ruins, and political claims.
Magic is known and influential but exceptional enough that famous mages, cults, relics, and lost sites matter.
Adventurers are common enough to be recognized but not trusted automatically.
The setting's famous NPCs should remain background powers unless the campaign naturally intersects them.
The 576 CY map is a starting situation, not a command to reenact later published wars.
gameMasterGuidance: Default to 576 CY and ask before applying later Greyhawk Wars or Living Greyhawk events.
Use political borders as claims whose enforcement varies across roads, forests, hills, and frontier settlements.
Keep the Free City cosmopolitan, commercially powerful, and politically limited.
Treat famous wizards and demigods as distant forces rather than substitute protagonists.
Use local cults, nobles, guilds, mercenaries, temples, and petty rulers to carry most play.
Distinguish ethnic history, modern nationality, language, and personal identity.
Make ruins culturally specific rather than labeling every old site Suel.
Preserve uncertainty where the 2024 presentation invites customization.
Use classic material for detail without importing later political outcomes.
Mark new settlements, officeholders, and campaign outcomes as campaign-created.
canonBoundaries: Do not treat the Flanaess as the whole world of Oerth.
Do not blend 576 CY with post-Greyhawk-Wars borders and rulers.
Do not make the Free City of Greyhawk a continental government.
Do not assume every famous module or adventure has occurred.
Do not make Iuz omnipresent outside his sphere of influence.
Do not treat the Great Kingdom as a stable unified empire in 576 CY.
Do not reduce Baklunish, Suel, Flan, or Oeridian heritage to alignment or personality.
Do not turn every humanoid realm into a faceless monster wilderness.
Do not import Forgotten Realms gods, cities, or institutions.
When old and new presentations differ, follow the selected era and state the adaptation.

referenceChunks.title: Oerth, Oerik, and the Flanaess
referenceChunks.text: Oerth is the world of the Greyhawk setting. Most published campaigns focus on the Flanaess, the eastern portion of the continent Oerik. The Flanaess contains seas, mountain ranges, great rivers, forests, fertile plains, deserts, marshes, islands, and many independent states. It is not the whole planet, and even Oerik extends far beyond the familiar map. The setting's geography encourages regional campaigns. The central Flanaess contains the Free City of Greyhawk, the Cairn Hills, the Domain of Greyhawk, the Wild Coast, the Pomarj, and nearby states. The north contains Iuz, Furyondy, the Shield Lands, the Bandit Kingdoms, the Theocracy of the Pale, and cold or frontier territories. The east includes the remnants of the Great Kingdom, Nyrond, the Iron League, the Sea Barons, and the Solnor coast. The south contains Keoland, Ulek states, the Hold of the Sea Princes, the Amedio Jungle, Hepmonaland approaches, and the Tilvanot Peninsula. The west leads toward Baklunish states, the Dry Steppes, and the Sea of Dust. Political maps exaggerate control. A kingdom can claim forest, hill, or borderland that it patrols only seasonally. Roads, rivers, passes, forts, and market towns matter more than colored borders. Monsters, humanoid realms, old ruins, and local lords occupy gaps between governments. The 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide presents the Flanaess as a world near a boiling point, with several mass conflicts ready to erupt. Use that pressure without assuming a future war's outcome. A local tax dispute, missing patrol, ruined keep, or cult can become important because neighboring powers are already nervous.

referenceChunks.title: Migrations and Cultural History
referenceChunks.text: The peoples of the Flanaess descend from many migrations and older civilizations. Four broad human cultural-historical groupings appear frequently in classic sources: Flan, Oeridian, Suel, and Baklunish. These categories describe complex histories and mixtures, not biological destinies or one culture per person. Flan peoples lived across much of the Flanaess before later migrations and maintain varied traditions, languages, states, and communities. Oeridian migrations contributed to many central and eastern kingdoms, including old imperial structures. Suel refugees moved east after magical catastrophe destroyed their ancient empire. Baklunish civilizations and nomadic peoples occupy western lands and preserve their own states, faiths, and scholarly traditions. The ancient Suel and Baklunish empires destroyed each other through magical catastrophe. The Invoked Devastation ruined Baklunish lands, while the Rain of Colorless Fire turned the Suel Imperium into the Sea of Dust. Survivors migrated, carrying enemies, religions, magic, and aristocratic claims into new lands. Modern populations are mixed. National identity, city, class, faith, and family often matter more than a distant ancestry. Keoland, Furyondy, Nyrond, the Great Kingdom, and the Free City each combine several heritages. Use historical identity to explain language, architecture, ruins, inherited law, and political memory. Do not use it as a substitute for characterization or moral alignment. A noble's claim to pure lineage may be propaganda serving property and status.

referenceChunks.title: Calendar and the 576 CY Baseline
referenceChunks.editionScope: 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide and classic Greyhawk
referenceChunks.text: Greyhawk commonly uses the Common Year calendar, abbreviated CY. The default setting year is 576 CY, a classic point before the major changes of the Greyhawk Wars. The 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide deliberately returns to this baseline so Game Masters can develop conflicts rather than inherit every later outcome. The Flanaess contains several calendars and regional naming traditions. The common calendar has twelve lunar months arranged into four seasonal quarters, with festival weeks between them. Needfest marks midwinter, Growfest spring, Richfest midsummer, and Brewfest autumn. Major cities and governments use dates for contracts, taxes, military service, and religious observance, while villages may describe time through planting, market days, and local saints. Later products advance the timeline into and beyond the Greyhawk Wars. By those dates, rulers have died, borders shifted, and states fallen or recovered. Never mention a later political fact as if it were already true in 576 CY. A year label should appear whenever recent politics matter. Ancient ruins and geography can be used across eras, but active rulers, alliances, military occupation, and faction strength require the selected date. The traditional named years and prophetic associations can provide flavor, but they do not dictate campaign events. The 576 CY baseline is valuable precisely because several futures remain possible. Player actions can prevent a war, cause one, or redirect which powers rise.

referenceChunks.title: The Free City of Greyhawk
referenceChunks.editionScope: 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide and classic city sources
referenceChunks.text: The Free City of Greyhawk stands on the River Selintan near the Nyr Dyv and serves as a major commercial, political, and adventuring center. Its location connects river traffic, roads, nearby mines, farms, ruins, and frontier regions. The city controls a modest surrounding domain but is not a nation governing the Flanaess. Government traditionally rests with a Directing Oligarchy whose members represent wealth, guilds, military interests, law, and influential institutions. Exact membership varies by source and era. The Lord Mayor acts within this oligarchic system rather than as an unchecked monarch. The city contains distinct quarters, markets, temples, guilds, universities, inns, warehouses, criminal networks, noble residences, poor districts, and nearby settlements. Its Thieves' Guild is an established political force, while the City Watch, courts, guilds, and private power compete over enforcement. Greyhawk's prosperity comes partly from adventurers and the treasures they bring from Castle Greyhawk, the Cairn Hills, old battlefields, and distant expeditions. Merchants, fences, sages, priests, mercenaries, and con artists all profit from that traffic. Famous residents can include mages, guild leaders, and figures known across the setting, but an ordinary campaign should build its own local patrons. The city should feel independent, practical, crowded, and opportunistic. It welcomes money more readily than strangers and tolerates adventurers because their danger feeds the economy. Use civic politics through permits, guild claims, taxation, crime, news, property, and neighborhood relationships. Greyhawk is a launch point and a place worth changing, not merely the tavern outside a dungeon.

referenceChunks.title: The Central Flanaess
referenceChunks.text: The central Flanaess surrounding Greyhawk is politically fragmented and rich in adventure sites. The Cairn Hills contain mines, tombs, old settlements, monsters, and communities linked to the Free City's economy. The Gnarley Forest and Kron Hills hold woods, villages, nonhuman communities, ruins, and contested routes. Dyvers is a rival free city on the Nyr Dyv with its own trade interests. Verbobonc is a viscounty associated with nearby villages, roads, and the aftermath or possibility of cult activity at the Temple of Elemental Evil. Do not assume a famous temple adventure has already occurred. The Wild Coast contains independent towns, petty rulers, pirates, mercenaries, and unstable law. South of it, the Pomarj is controlled by humanoid powers and raiders in the 576 CY framework. These realms have politics and logistics; they are not endless encounter tables. Celene is an elven kingdom with strong traditions and an often isolationist policy. The Ulek states include dwarven, elven, and mixed realms with distinct governments and interests. Relations among these powers shape defense against the Pomarj and influence trade. The region supports short travel between very different jurisdictions. A road can pass from city law to noble territory, forest custom, bandit control, and disputed frontier. Use that variety to make local knowledge important. Famous modules are associated with this region, but their locations should be treated as available sites rather than completed history unless the campaign chooses otherwise.

referenceChunks.title: Furyondy, Iuz, and the Northern Frontier
referenceChunks.text: Furyondy is a powerful northern kingdom descended from the old Viceroyalty of Ferrond. It faces sustained danger from Iuz and neighboring hostile powers while managing nobles, provinces, trade, and relations with Veluna and the Highfolk. Iuz is a demigod tyrant whose realm lies to the north. His rule combines personal cult, evil priesthood, humanoid armies, oppression, magic, and opportunistic expansion. In 576 CY his power is serious but should not be projected across every northern village as perfect control. The Shield Lands form a frontier of nobles, knights, forts, and settlements exposed to threats from Iuz, the Horned Society, and the Bandit Kingdoms. The Horned Society is a separate hostile power with its own leadership and territory in this baseline. Later timelines change these conditions. The Vesve Forest, Highfolk, and nearby lands contain elves, humans, gnomes, rangers, settlements, and routes whose allegiance cannot be reduced to one kingdom. The Bandit Kingdoms are a patchwork of rulers and territories rather than one nation. Northern play should involve intelligence, patrols, refugees, fortification, cults, raids, noble rivalry, and uncertainty over whether a local crisis is connected to a larger offensive. Iuz can act through agents and fear without appearing personally. Do not import later conquests from the Greyhawk Wars into 576 CY. The tension lies in what may happen, and the characters can materially alter the frontier.

referenceChunks.title: The Great Kingdom and the Eastern Flanaess
referenceChunks.text: The Great Kingdom of Aerdy once dominated much of the eastern Flanaess. By 576 CY it is a decaying imperial structure marked by cruel rulers, powerful nobles, provincial ambition, military orders, and declining central authority. Overking Ivid V rules from Rauxes in the classic baseline, but actual control varies across provinces. The Great Kingdom should not be portrayed as a healthy centralized empire. Noble houses, church interests, military commanders, cities, and frontier lords maintain their own agendas. The state can still field armies and inspire fear while losing the capacity to govern evenly. Nyrond broke from the old empire and became a major eastern kingdom. It faces military pressure, economic burdens, and regional responsibilities. The Iron League links several southern and coastal states in resistance to Aerdy power, though its members retain separate interests. Almor, Onnwal, Idee, Sunndi, the County and Duchy of Urnst, the Sea Barons, and other eastern states create a dense political map. The Bone March contains hostile powers and contested ruins. The Adri and Grandwood forests shelter communities, rebels, monsters, and independent interests. In play, imperial documents and titles can remain legally powerful long after practical control has failed. A noble may claim taxes from land occupied by rebels. A garrison may obey an old order because no replacement arrived. Later Greyhawk sources radically change the Great Kingdom. Do not introduce those outcomes in 576 CY unless the campaign advances toward them.

referenceChunks.title: Keoland and the Southwestern Flanaess
referenceChunks.text: Keoland is one of the oldest surviving kingdoms in the Flanaess and a major power of the southwest. Its history includes expansion, contraction, relations with neighboring peoples, and competing visions of royal authority. By 576 CY it remains influential without controlling every former possession. The Yeomanry is known for citizen soldiers and a political tradition distinct from hereditary monarchy. Geoff and Sterich lie near giant-haunted mountains and frontier lands. The Gran March maintains strong military traditions. Bissel occupies a strategic route between eastern and western powers. The Ulek states include the Principality of Ulek, County of Ulek, and Duchy of Ulek, each with different populations and governments. Celene and the Lortmil Mountains influence regional politics and defense. The Hold of the Sea Princes is a maritime and plantation power associated with piracy, slavery, and coastal trade. The Amedio Jungle and Hellfurnaces lie beyond settled borders and contain local peoples, ruins, monsters, and competing expeditions. Do not portray them as empty exploration zones. Southwestern campaigns can involve giant raids, court politics, maritime crime, abolition, border defense, dwarven trade, elven isolation, and old Suel sites. Later sources bring major wars and occupations to parts of the region; keep those as possible futures in 576 CY. Keoland should feel historically deep and administratively real, with provincial nobles, towns, roads, temples, and old claims, rather than simply the safe kingdom beside adventure territory.

referenceChunks.title: The Baklunish West and the Sea of Dust
referenceChunks.text: Western Flanaess lands preserve Baklunish states, nomadic traditions, trade routes, faiths, and memories of the ancient magical war with the Suel Imperium. Ekbir, Zeif, Tusmit, Ket, Ull, the Plains of the Paynims, and nearby territories differ in government, economy, and culture. Ket occupies a strategic position between western and central lands and can mediate or contest trade. Ekbir and Zeif represent important settled powers. The Paynims include many nomadic peoples and confederations rather than one tribe. Ull is associated with harsher rule and frontier danger, but local inhabitants still possess ordinary communities and interests. The Dry Steppes and mountain routes connect nomadic, settled, and distant lands. The Sea of Dust marks the ruined heart of the ancient Suel Imperium after the Rain of Colorless Fire. Expeditions face environmental danger, lost cities, magical residue, and rival claims. Baklunish cultures should not be reduced to desert stereotypes or one religion. Use specific states, professions, family structures, trade practices, and local law. Western scholars, priests, soldiers, merchants, and nomads possess different relationships to ancient history. The Invoked Devastation and Rain of Colorless Fire remain central collective memories. They can shape attitudes toward destructive magic and Suel ruins without requiring modern people to inherit ancient guilt. Classic sources describe the west less deeply than central regions. When adding detail, mark it as campaign-created and avoid presenting generalized real-world borrowing as Greyhawk canon.

referenceChunks.title: The Scarlet Brotherhood and the Southern Seas
referenceChunks.text: The Scarlet Brotherhood is a secretive and dangerous organization based on the Tilvanot Peninsula. It promotes a supremacist interpretation of Suel heritage and pursues influence through spies, assassins, monks, agents, manipulation, and long planning. Its ideology is villainous and should not be treated as an accurate account of Suel history or culture. In 576 CY, much of the Brotherhood's reach is hidden. Later timelines reveal major operations and territorial gains. Do not import those later successes automatically. A local official may be an agent, a dupe, a target, or falsely accused. The southern seas connect the Flanaess to islands, the Amedio Jungle, Hepmonaland, trade routes, pirates, and communities outside the best-known map. The Lordship of the Isles and Hold of the Sea Princes have their own maritime politics. Olman and other southern peoples possess civilizations, histories, and claims that should not be treated as exotic ruins for northern adventurers. Adventures involving the Brotherhood work through evidence, coded networks, ideological recruitment, and institutional vulnerability. Not every conspiracy should secretly lead to it. The organization becomes less credible if it controls all events. Use supremacist ideology carefully. Present its harm and falsehood without reproducing it as neutral cultural description. Individual Suel-descended characters and states are not responsible for or aligned with the Brotherhood.

referenceChunks.title: Gods and Religion
referenceChunks.text: Greyhawk has a broad pantheon associated with several cultural traditions and widespread faiths. Well-known deities include Pelor, Heironeous, Hextor, Nerull, St. Cuthbert, Rao, Pholtus, Ehlonna, Obad-Hai, Fharlanghn, Boccob, Wee Jas, Kord, Olidammara, and many others. Iuz is both a ruler and demigod. Some gods have strong regional or ethnic associations while being worshipped elsewhere. Temples provide ritual, charity, healing, law, education, military orders, pilgrimage, and political influence. A church is not a perfectly unified expression of a god. Heironean knights, Pelorian healers, Cuthbertine judges, and Pholtan theocrats can disagree internally and across regions. Rival divine portfolios can reinforce political conflict, especially Heironeous and Hextor, or Rao's peace traditions and militant states. Evil cults may be illegal, hidden, tolerated, or politically protected depending on jurisdiction. Greyhawk's deities were incorporated into broader D&D material, but the setting's regional context matters. Do not import a Forgotten Realms church hierarchy because a deity's rules appear in the same game. Ordinary people may honor several gods according to need. Clerics and paladins are exceptional, while many priests possess no adventuring powers. Divine magic confirms supernatural reality without making every doctrinal claim infallible. Use faith through holidays, burial, oaths, law, land, and social service, not only combat powers.

referenceChunks.title: Magic, Famous Mages, and Artifacts
referenceChunks.text: Greyhawk is home to many figures and artifacts that became iconic across Dungeons & Dragons. Mordenkainen and the Circle of Eight pursue balance and intervene in threats according to their own judgments. Other famous mages, including Bigby, Tenser, Otiluke, and Rary, have specific histories that vary by date. In 576 CY, do not import later betrayals or deaths prematurely. Vecna originated as a lich and ancient tyrant associated with the Flanaess, while artifacts such as the Hand and Eye of Vecna spread far beyond the setting. Acererak and the Tomb of Horrors are also connected to Greyhawk. Their fame does not require them to be behind every undead or dungeon. Magic is powerful but socially uneven. Courts, temples, guilds, isolated wizards, cults, elves, ancient civilizations, and adventurers preserve different traditions. Magic items and spellcasters exist without creating a continent of effortless teleportation and resurrection. Ancient artifacts often carry political and religious claims. A sword can legitimize a dynasty, a seal open an imperial vault, or a relic attract several churches. Their history should matter as much as statistics. Use famous mages as distant patrons, rivals, theories, or historical influences. Player characters should not report to the Circle of Eight by default. The existence of powerful NPCs creates politics, not a reason they solve every crisis. When a spell or item bears a famous name, it does not prove every character knows the inventor's biography.

referenceChunks.title: Humanoids, Nonhumans, and Frontier Politics
referenceChunks.editionScope: Current inclusive presentation with classic foundations
referenceChunks.text: The Flanaess contains human, elven, dwarven, gnomish, halfling, orc, goblin, hobgoblin, giant, and many other communities. Classic maps often label regions through dominant populations or hostile forces, but a species label is not a complete political description. Elven states such as Celene and nonhuman realms in the Ulek region have distinct governments, interests, and internal disagreements. Dwarven and gnomish communities control mines, roads, hills, and fortresses while trading with neighboring states. Mixed cities are common along major routes. The Pomarj and Bone March include powerful humanoid forces, but their rulers require food, labor, alliances, succession, and logistics. Orcs and goblinoids can be soldiers, subjects, traders, rebels, mercenaries, and civilians rather than one alignment category. Giants, dragons, and other beings can rule territory or maintain old claims. Frontier humans may commit raids and atrocities as readily as nonhuman neighbors. The 2024 rules reject species-wide moral alignment as destiny. Preserve canonical hostile regimes and cults without turning every member of a people into a combatant. When creating an encounter, identify affiliation before ancestry. A goblin messenger from one realm, an orc deserter from another, and a human slaver from a third create more Greyhawk politics than a generic 'monster patrol.'

referenceChunks.title: Adventuring, Dungeons, and Factions
referenceChunks.editionScope: 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide and classic Greyhawk
referenceChunks.text: Greyhawk is closely associated with dungeon exploration, dangerous ruins, wilderness expeditions, and factions competing over recovered power. Castle Greyhawk, the Temple of Elemental Evil, the Tomb of Horrors, the Ghost Tower of Inverness, White Plume Mountain, and many other sites belong to the setting's history or publication tradition. Their adventures are not automatically completed. Dungeons should have creators, later occupants, supply routes, faction interests, and consequences. A ruined Suel site differs from an Oeridian fortress, Flan burial place, cult temple, giant stronghold, or wizard's laboratory. Adventurers are recognized as useful and dangerous. Cities tax treasure, guilds and temples seek relics, nobles hire deniable specialists, and villagers remember collateral harm. Rival adventuring companies can compete without becoming villains. The 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide highlights several large conflicts that can support campaign arcs. Use them through local signs: recruitment, refugees, disrupted trade, spies, border forts, and propaganda. Players should encounter pressures before being told they must save the world. Factions include governments, cults, knightly orders, guilds, criminal networks, churches, secret societies, and powerful individuals. Give them limited information and internal division. Reward negotiation, mapping, research, logistics, and alliance alongside combat. Greyhawk's dungeon tradition is strongest when treasure changes the surface world.

referenceChunks.title: Common Greyhawk Canon Traps
referenceChunks.text: The main error is timeline blending. The 576 CY baseline precedes the Greyhawk Wars and many later changes. Do not use postwar borders, rulers, destroyed states, or Living Greyhawk outcomes unless selected. Greyhawk is the name of a city, surrounding domain, and campaign setting, but the world is Oerth and the principal mapped region is the Flanaess. The Free City does not rule the continent. Do not make every famous adventure historical fact. Do not place Mordenkainen, Vecna, Acererak, Iuz, or the Scarlet Brotherhood behind every problem. Their fame should not shrink the world. Cultural heritages such as Suel, Baklunish, Flan, and Oeridian are not alignments or pure biological groups. The Scarlet Brotherhood's supremacist claims are ideology, not neutral canon truth. Do not portray humanoid territories as empty monster zones. Preserve hostile states and violence while allowing political and individual variation. The 2024 presentation intentionally leaves room for customization. When it simplifies or adjusts classic lore, use it as the current baseline and label additional older detail carefully. Avoid importing Forgotten Realms institutions because both are D&D fantasy worlds. Greyhawk's fragmented politics, restrained cosmopolitan centers, and unresolved conflicts should retain their own texture. When uncertain, stay at the reliable regional level and create a marked campaign fact instead of a false canonical officeholder.
